newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Lower NZ growth seen in year to March 1997--NZIER.
newsitem.headline: Lower NZ growth seen in year to March 1997--NZIER.

text.p: The New Zealand Institute of Economic Research (NZIER) said on Monday it had revised down its economic growth forecast to 1.7 percent from 2.8 percent for the year to March 1997.

NZIER said the change largely reflected lower private consumption growth. In addition, lower expectations of house price increases had hurt consumer confidence and would translate into lower growth in household spending.

The medium-term growth outlook remains "robust", NZIER said, predicting 3.6 percent in the March 1998 year thanks to a second round of tax cuts planned by the conservative National Party government for July 1997.
Growth would then average 2.9 percent in the next three years, the forecaster said.
It cautioned that this was based on the assumption of a centre-right coalition being returned to power after a general election next month.
"A change to a centre-left coalition on October 12 may result in higher short-term growth, but longer-term prospects may be less positive," it said.
Opinion polls suggest a centre-left coalition is somewhat more likely than a win for the centre-right.

NZIER said this could mean a lower exchange rate in the immediate election aftermath if overseas investors withdrew money. This could be offset or reversed if the central Reserve Bank raised interest rates.

Government spending, especially on health, education and welfare, was likely to rise under a centre-left government, though this could be offset to some extent by the scrapping of the second round of tax cuts.
A centre-left government was also expected to raise the central bank's zero to two percent underlying inflation target and adjust labour market legislation to give more bargaining power to employees.
"The programme to reduce tariffs may be slowed or halted. In addition, there may be tighter controls on immigration and on foreign ownership of property and enterprises," NZIER said.
Short-term growth could be higher due to the boost in public and private sector consumption from higher government spending.
"Longer term growth prospects are less clear, although regulatory changes are likely to lower business confidence and have a negative impact on investment and growth."
